title: Type System & Null Safety Basics
scopeHtml: Scope: the Any/Unit/Nothing hierarchy, Nothing in expressions, Unit vs Void, how null safety is compiled, safe call / elvis / !!, smart-cast rules, platform types and the nullability annotations Kotlin honors. Facts checked against kotlinlang.org (Kotlin 2.x docs).

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through Kotlin's type hierarchy. Where do Any, Any?, Unit, Nothing and Nothing? sit, and what does each map to on the JVM?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you see Kotlin's types as a lattice with a top and a bottom, or just as syntax. Everything else in null safety and generics builds on this.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Any? is the top type: every value, null included, is an Any?. Any is the top of non-null types and maps to java.lang.Object. Every non-null type T is a subtype of its nullable twin T?. At the bottom is Nothing, which has no values and is a subtype of every type, so an expression that never completes, such as throw, fits anywhere. Nothing? has exactly one value, null, which is why null can go into any nullable type. Unit is just an ordinary singleton object that means 'no useful result'. It is not the bottom type."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Think of types as sets of values. A subtype is a subset.

                    Any?                 <- top: all values + null
                  /      \
               Any        (all T?)       <- Any = java.lang.Object
             /  |  \        |
        String Int Unit ... String? Int? ...
             \  |  /        |
              (all T)       |
                  \        /
                  Nothing?               <- exactly one value: null
                     |
                  Nothing                <- bottom: no values at all
  • Any: declares only equals, hashCode and toString. On the JVM it is Object. Methods like wait/notify are not visible unless you cast to java.lang.Object (the cast is legal, but you rarely want it).
  • T vs T?: these are different types to the compiler. On the JVM, though, a reference String and a String? are both just java.lang.String. Nullability lives in Kotlin metadata, annotations (@NotNull/@Nullable are emitted for Java tools) and the inserted runtime checks (Q006). Primitives are different: Int becomes int, while Int? becomes a boxed java.lang.Integer. Boxing is chunk K1b's topic.
  • Unit: an object with one instance. Functions declared to return Unit compile to JVM void. See Q003.
  • Nothing: a class with a private constructor, so no instance can ever exist. A function returning Nothing must throw or loop forever. On the JVM, a Nothing return type compiles to java.lang.Void. See Q005.
  • Nothing?: the type of the literal null. val x = null infers x: Nothing?. Because Nothing? is a subtype of every T?, null can be assigned to any nullable type with no special rule.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val a: Any = "text"          // OK: String <: Any
val b: Any? = null           // OK: Nothing? <: Any?
// val c: Any = null         // compile error: Nothing? is not <: Any

val n = null                 // inferred type: Nothing?
val s: String? = n           // OK

fun fail(msg: String): Nothing = throw IllegalStateException(msg)
val port: Int = System.getenv("PORT")?.toInt() ?: fail("PORT missing") // Nothing <: Int

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling Unit the bottom type, or saying it is "like Nothing". Unit has a value, Nothing has none.
  • Thinking String? is a wrapper like Optional<String>. For reference types there is no wrapper object at runtime. For Int? there is, because of boxing.
  • Thinking Any maps to Any? on the JVM. Both are Object. The difference exists only at compile time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can emptyList() be assigned to List<String>? → It is List<Nothing> under the hood, and List is covariant. See the generics chunk.
  2. Is Nothing the same as Java void? → No. void means "returns without a value", which is Unit in Kotlin. Nothing means "never returns".
  3. Why does Kotlin need a bottom type at all? → So throw, return and TODO() can be expressions. val x = y ?: throw E() type-checks only because Nothing is a subtype of the type of y.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists the types. The senior draws the lattice, says that nullability is erased on the JVM except for primitives and runtime checks, and links Nothing to how expressions like ?: return type-check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that assume String? costs a wrapper sometimes add premature "optimizations". Teams that forget Int? does box pay real allocation cost in hot loops.

questions.promptHtml: Explain ?., ?: and !!. What type does each expression have, and when is each one the right tool?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is a basic screen, but the follow-ups (types, evaluation order, how often you reach for !!) quickly separate careful engineers from people who silence the compiler.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "a?.b evaluates a. If a is null the whole expression is null and b is never touched. Otherwise it accesses b. The result is always nullable. a ?: b returns a if it is not null, otherwise it evaluates b, lazily. The result type is the common supertype of non-null A and B. Because throw and return have type Nothing, ?: return and ?: throw narrow the value to non-null. a!! turns A? into A and throws a NullPointerException if it is null. I use !! only where null would be a programmer error and I want a crash right at that line. Anything that comes from I/O, Java or the user gets a safe call or elvis."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Operator Evaluates RHS when Result type On null
a?.foo() a != null R? whole chain yields null
a ?: b a == null LUB(A, B) (non-null if B is non-null) yields b
a!! — A throws NullPointerException
a as? T — T? null (cast topic, see K1b)
  • Safe calls short-circuit along a chain: in user?.address?.city, if user is null nothing to the right runs.
  • With a safe call on the left side of an assignment, a?.x = compute(), compute() is not called when a is null. This is documented behavior and it surprises people (see Q009).
  • ?: is right-associative: a ?: b ?: c means a ?: (b ?: c).
  • !! compiles to a null check that throws a Kotlin NPE (Intrinsics.checkNotNull in recent compilers). The stack trace points at the !! line, which is the one good thing about it.
  • ?.let { } runs a block only for non-null values. Choosing between scope functions belongs to chunk K4.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun displayName(user: User?): String =
    user?.profile?.nickname        // String?
        ?: user?.email             // String?
        ?: "Guest"                 // String: the last operand is non-null, so the result is non-null

fun load(id: String?) {
    val safeId = id ?: return      // safeId: String from here on
    repo.fetch(safeId)
}

val cfg = configOrNull()!!         // broken in prod paths: crashes with an NPE and no context
val cfg2 = requireNotNull(configOrNull()) { "config not loaded before onCreate" } // same crash, readable message

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Chaining !! (a!!.b!!.c!!). You get a crash with no clue which link was null when several sit on one line.
  • Expecting ?. to return a non-null value. You need an elvis at the end to get T.
  • Using ?. to skip a side effect that was not supposed to be optional. The bug disappears silently instead of failing loudly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's the type of x ?: throw E()? → The non-null type of x, because throw is Nothing.
  2. !! vs requireNotNull vs checkNotNull? → All three throw on null. requireNotNull throws IllegalArgumentException (a bad argument), checkNotNull throws IllegalStateException (bad state), and both take a lazy message. !! throws an NPE with no message.
  3. Does ?. add allocation or overhead? → No. It compiles to a plain if (a != null) branch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer describes what the operators do. The senior gives the result types, mentions that the RHS is evaluated lazily, explains why ?: return narrows, and has a clear policy for !! (assertion of an invariant, with a message, never on external data).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A typical crash-free-rate regression is an !! on a Bundle or intent extra that "is always set", until a deep link or process-death restore arrives without it.

questions.promptHtml: What is Unit and how is it different from Java's void and Void?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know why Kotlin made "no result" a real type, and whether you have hit the Java-interop pain this causes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Unit is a real type with exactly one value, the Unit object. A Kotlin function returning Unit compiles to JVM void, so normal calls cost nothing. Because it is a real type, it works as a type argument: () -> Unit is Function0<Unit>, and Deferred<Unit> is fine. Java void is not a type, so you can't write List<void>. Java's Void is a type, but its only legal value is null, so it is closer to Kotlin's Nothing?. The practical pain is Java code implementing a Kotlin lambda: it has to return Unit.INSTANCE;."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Declaration: public object Unit { override fun toString() = "kotlin.Unit" }.
  • When the compiler emits void vs Unit: if a function's declared return type is exactly Unit (or omitted for a block body), it is compiled as void. When Unit shows up through a generic, for example overriding fun get(): T with T = Unit or calling invoke() on a Function0<Unit>, the JVM signature returns Object and the code actually returns Unit.INSTANCE.
  • Every lambda whose last expression has some type but whose expected type is () -> Unit has its result discarded and Unit returned (Unit coercion).
Kotlin Unit Java void Java Void
Is a type usable in generics yes no yes
Values Unit singleton none only null
Kotlin analog — Unit (in return position) Nothing?

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Kotlin API
fun setListener(onDone: (String) -> Unit) { /* ... */ }
// Java caller: has to return Unit.INSTANCE
setListener(s -> { log(s); return Unit.INSTANCE; });
// Interop-friendly alternative: a fun interface with a Unit return compiles to a void SAM method
fun interface DoneListener { fun onDone(result: String) }
fun setListener(listener: DoneListener) { /* ... */ }
// Java: setListener(s -> log(s));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Unit is like void" and stopping there. The type-argument part is what matters.
  • Writing a generic API as Callback<Void?> in Kotlin to mirror Java. Use Unit in Kotlin-first code.
  • Exposing Kotlin function types to Java consumers in a public SDK without thinking about Unit.INSTANCE and Function1 imports.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does println(println("x")) print? → x and then kotlin.Unit.
  2. Why does suspend fun foo() sometimes return Unit.INSTANCE in bytecode? → After the CPS transform, a suspend function returns Any?, so it can't be void. It returns either COROUTINE_SUSPENDED or Unit. See the coroutines CPS chunk.
  3. Unit vs Nothing in one line? → Unit returns normally with nothing interesting. Nothing never returns.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says Unit equals void. The senior explains the dual compilation (void vs Unit.INSTANCE in generic or lambda positions), relates Void to Nothing?, and designs Java-friendly APIs with fun interface.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: SDK teams shipping Kotlin libraries to Java-heavy clients get "why do I need to return Unit.INSTANCE" tickets. fun interface callbacks avoid that.

questions.promptHtml: What is a platform type, what does String! mean, and why didn't Kotlin just treat every Java type as nullable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most real Android code still crosses Java boundaries: framework, SDKs, legacy modules. Platform types are where Kotlin's null safety stops guaranteeing anything.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When Kotlin sees a Java type with no nullability information, it gives it a platform type, written T! in IDE hints and error messages. You can't write it in source. It means 'the nullability is unknown'. The compiler lets you use it as either T or T?, and it does not check. If you treat it as non-null and it is null, you get an NPE. That's either at the dereference, or earlier, at an inserted check, if you assign it to a declared non-null type. Kotlin chose this over 'everything is nullable' because that would force !! or ?. on every Java call, including generics like ArrayList<String?>, and the language would be unusable with Java."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The notations Kotlin shows: T! means T or T?. (Mutable)Collection<T>! means a Java collection that may be mutable or not, and nullable or not. Array<(out) T>! is a Java array of T or a subtype.
  • Inference propagates platform types: val name = javaUser.getName() gives name: String!. The unknown nullability now spreads into your Kotlin code and fails at whatever line first dereferences it.
  • Declaring the type pins it down: val name: String = javaUser.getName() makes the compiler insert a check at assignment time, so the failure happens at the boundary with a clear message (Q006). val name: String? = ... makes you handle null explicitly.
  • Annotations remove platform types. If the Java side is annotated with a supported annotation (Q011), Kotlin sees a real String or String?.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Java: public String getToken() { return token; }   // no annotation
val t1 = sdk.getToken()            // String!  (danger spreads)
t1.length                          // NPE here if null; the stack points deep in your code

val t2: String = sdk.getToken()    // fails right here: "getToken(...) must not be null"
val t3: String? = sdk.getToken()   // safest: compiler now forces you to handle null

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting inference keep T! and passing the value through three layers before it crashes.
  • Overriding a Java method in Kotlin and choosing non-null parameter types when the framework may pass null. The inserted parameter check then crashes.
  • Assuming Android framework types are always platform types. Much of android.jar is annotated now (Q011), so types often arrive already nullable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does a Java List<String> look like in Kotlin? → (Mutable)List<String!>!. Both the list and its elements have unknown nullability.
  2. Where exactly does the NPE get thrown? → Either at the dereference (a JVM NPE) or at an inserted Intrinsics check when the value is assigned or passed to a non-null Kotlin type.
  3. How would you make a whole Java module safe? → Annotate it, ideally with JSpecify @NullMarked, and raise strictness. See Q011 and Q014.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "String! means it might be null." The senior explains why the trade-off exists, describes how inference spreads the problem, and states a boundary policy: declare an explicit type at the Java seam, annotate the Java side, and treat SDK returns as nullable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Many "impossible" Kotlin NPEs in Crashlytics trace back to a platform-typed value from a Java SDK that crashed far from where it entered the code.

questions.promptHtml: Show me how Nothing works in everyday code: throw, TODO(), ?: return, functions that never return. What does the compiler do with it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows that you understand control flow as part of the type system, not as a special case.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "throw, return, break and continue are expressions of type Nothing. Because Nothing is a subtype of everything, they can sit in any expression slot, such as an elvis right-hand side, an if branch or a when branch, without changing the result type. The compiler also does flow analysis: after an expression of type Nothing, the code is unreachable. So after val x = y ?: return, x is non-null, and after a call to a function returning Nothing you get an 'unreachable code' warning. TODO() and error() are just stdlib functions returning Nothing."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Type of a conditional: if (c) a else b has type LUB(A, B). If B is Nothing, the LUB is A. That is why val n: Int = if (ok) 1 else throw E() compiles.
  • In when, an else -> error("unexpected $x") branch keeps the result type clean.
  • Smart-cast interaction: if (x == null) return and x ?: return both make x (or the new val) non-null afterward, because the null path ends in Nothing.
  • Your own functions: declare : Nothing explicitly. If you write fun fail() { throw E() }, the return type is Unit, and the compiler can no longer prove that the code after it is unreachable or smart-cast across it.
  • Stdlib helpers that return Nothing: TODO(reason) throws NotImplementedError, which extends Error rather than Exception (see Q015). error(msg) throws IllegalStateException.
  • JVM detail: a Nothing return type compiles to java.lang.Void. Java callers see a method that returns Void, and Java does not know it never returns.
  • Nothing? vs Nothing: a function returning Nothing? can return normally (with null), so it gives no unreachability.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun fail(msg: String): Nothing = throw IllegalStateException(msg)   // explicit Nothing matters
fun failUnit(msg: String) { throw IllegalStateException(msg) }      // inferred Unit: loses flow info

fun parse(raw: String?): Int {
    val s = raw ?: fail("raw is null")      // s: String
    return when {
        s.isEmpty() -> 0
        s.all(Char::isDigit) -> s.toInt()
        else -> error("bad input: $s")      // Nothing fits the Int branch
    }
}

fun broken(raw: String?): Int {
    if (raw == null) failUnit("null")
    return raw.length                       // compile error: raw is still String?
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving out : Nothing on a throwing helper and then sprinkling !! after calls to it.
  • Assuming TODO() is a compile-time marker. It compiles fine and throws at runtime, as an Error.
  • Putting ?: return inside a lambda without thinking about which function it returns from. That is a labels and non-local-return topic, see chunk K3a.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What type does val x = throw E() have? → Nothing. The compiler warns that the code after it is unreachable.
  2. Can a Nothing function contain while (true) {} instead of throw? → Yes. Any function body that never completes normally type-checks.
  3. How do contracts relate? → require(cond) smart-casts with returns() implies cond contracts. That is a different mechanism from Nothing (chunk K9). Nothing is built into the type system, while contracts are opt-in annotations on functions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "Nothing is for functions that throw." The senior explains LUB typing of branches, flow-based unreachability and smart casts, why the explicit : Nothing annotation matters, and the JVM Void mapping.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Throwing helpers such as crashWithLog() that return Unit show up again and again in code review. They force !! after every call and make reviewers nervous for no reason.

questions.promptHtml: Kotlin types are erased to plain JVM references. So how is null safety enforced at runtime? What does the compiler actually insert?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors read stack traces like Parameter specified as non-null is null and need to know which line created the check, why it exists, and what turning it off would cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Null safety is mostly compile-time. At the boundaries where Java can sneak in a null, the compiler inserts calls to kotlin.jvm.internal.Intrinsics. Every non-private function gets checkNotNullParameter for each non-null reference parameter, because Java or reflection could call it with null. When a platform-typed Java result is stored in, or passed as, a non-null Kotlin type, the compiler inserts checkNotNullExpressionValue, which gives the 'getX(...) must not be null' message. !! compiles to a plain null check that throws. Since Kotlin 1.4 these all throw NullPointerException. Private functions skip the parameter check, because only Kotlin code that has already been type-checked can call them."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Situation Inserted check (Kotlin 1.4+) Message shape
Non-null param of a public/protected/internal function Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(p, "p") at function entry Parameter specified as non-null is null: method com.x.Foo.bar, parameter p
Platform expression assigned to a non-null type Intrinsics.checkNotNullExpressionValue(v, "getToken(...)") getToken(...) must not be null
x!! Intrinsics.checkNotNull(x) (or an equivalent inline throw) plain NPE
Extension receiver of a non-private function receiver check similar parameter message
  • Before Kotlin 1.4, the parameter checks threw IllegalArgumentException and the expression checks threw IllegalStateException. Kotlin 1.4 unified them on NullPointerException, so old crash-grouping rules may have changed.
  • Compiler flags exist to remove them: -Xno-param-assertions, -Xno-call-assertions, -Xno-receiver-assertions. They are not recommended. See Q018 for the trade-off.
  • Cost: a static call and a compare per parameter. The JIT/ART AOT normally inlines that to almost nothing. The main cost is bytecode size and the parameter-name string constants, which R8 can shrink.
  • What is not checked: private functions, local functions, values a Java caller writes directly into a non-private Kotlin field (@JvmField), values set by reflection (Gson, Unsafe, see chunk K1b), and generic type arguments (a List<String> can contain nulls inserted by Java).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Repo {
    fun save(id: String) { /* ... */ }        // gets checkNotNullParameter(id, "id")
    private fun log(msg: String) { /* ... */ } // no check
}

// Decompiled (simplified)
// public final void save(@NotNull String id) {
//     Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(id, "id");
//     ...
// }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the crash means "Kotlin has a bug". The check fired exactly where Java violated the contract, which is the most useful place it could fire.
  • Reading Parameter specified as non-null is null and fixing the Kotlin callee by making the param nullable everywhere, instead of fixing or annotating the Java caller.
  • Assuming a List<String> from Java has no nulls because the Kotlin type says so. Element nullability is never checked at runtime.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are private functions skipped? → All their callers are compiled Kotlin in the same class, already type-checked. A check would be pure overhead.
  2. Does internal get checks? → Yes. Internal functions are public in bytecode (with name mangling), so Java in the same module can call them.
  3. Does a lateinit access compile to a similar check? → Yes, it throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException. That belongs to the lateinit chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "Kotlin adds null checks." The senior names the specific Intrinsics, knows which function visibilities get them, knows the 1.4 exception type change, lists what is not covered (fields, reflection, generic contents), and uses the message format to find the offending boundary quickly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash groups titled checkNotNullParameter almost always point at a Java framework callback overridden with the wrong nullability, or at a Java caller. The stack frame right below the check is the culprit.

questions.promptHtml: When does Kotlin smart cast a value after an is or null check, and when does it refuse? Explain the reasoning behind each rule.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Smart cast is impossible" is a daily compiler error. Knowing why it fires tells the interviewer whether you understand stability, which is what keeps the compiler sound.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The compiler only smart casts when it can prove the value can't change between the check and the use. It calls such a value 'stable'. Local vals are always stable, except for local delegated properties, because a delegate's getValue can return anything. Local vars are stable if nothing modifies them between check and use, and no lambda that modifies them has captured them. A val property is stable only if it is private or internal, or is declared in the same module, and has no custom getter and isn't open. Each of those could make two reads return different values. A var property is never smart cast, since another thread or method can write to it. The fix is almost always to copy it into a local val first."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Value Smart cast? Why
local val yes assigned once, nobody else sees it
local delegated val x by lazy {} no getValue() is an arbitrary call each read
local var yes, if no write between check and use and not captured by a lambda that writes it flow analysis can prove it
val property, same module, final, default getter yes backed by a final field and the code ships together
val property with a custom get() no getter may compute a new value each time
open val no a subclass may override it with a getter
val property from another module (public) no that module could add a custom getter later without recompiling you (binary compatibility)
var property no concurrent or reentrant writes possible
  • In Kotlin 2.0 the K2 compiler widened smart casts. It keeps information through local Boolean variables (val isCat = x is Cat; if (isCat) ...), smart casts to the common supertype for || checks, tracks captured vars in inline lambdas, and carries information into catch/finally. The stability rules in the table did not change. K2 specifics are in chunk K8.
  • Smart casts are purely compile-time. No runtime cast is skipped or added. The bytecode still contains a CHECKCAST where the JVM needs one.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Screen(var user: User?) {
    fun render() {
        if (user != null) {
            // user.name                // error: 'user' is a mutable property that could have been changed
        }
        val u = user ?: return          // fix: snapshot into a stable local
        show(u.name)
    }
}

fun local() {
    var token: String? = fetch()
    if (token != null) {
        println(token.length)           // OK: no write in between
    }
    val job = Runnable { token = null } // capturing lambda that writes...
    if (token != null) {
        // println(token.length)        // ...now an error: concurrent modification is possible
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" the error with !!. That compiles and re-introduces exactly the race the compiler warned about (see Q008).
  • Believing smart casts fail because "the compiler is dumb". Each rule protects soundness against a real change path.
  • Moving a model class into a :core module and being surprised that all smart casts on its public vals break. See Q016.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not for open val? → A subclass can override it with get() = Random.nextInt()-style logic, so two reads might differ.
  2. Does ?.let { } avoid the problem? → Yes. it is a stable lambda parameter bound to a single read. A local val is usually more readable.
  3. Is an internal val in a different module stable? → internal is visible only within one module, so the question doesn't come up. Within the module, internal and private finals can be smart cast.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "Use a local val when the compiler complains." The senior gives the stability rationale for each row, especially the cross-module binary-compatibility one, and knows K2 extended the analysis without loosening the rules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Every !! added to get past a smart-cast error on a var property is a candidate TOCTOU crash. Reviewers should flag those first.

questions.subtopic: Smart cast vs `!!` on mutable properties
questions.contextHtml:
A news app (1.5M DAU, ~60% Android 12+) shipped release 8.4. Crash-free sessions dropped from 99.82% to 99.61%. The top new crash:

java.lang.NullPointerException
    at com.app.feed.FeedPresenter.renderHeader(FeedPresenter.kt:88)
    at com.app.feed.FeedPresenter.onFeedLoaded(FeedPresenter.kt:61)
    at com.app.feed.FeedRepository$load$1.onResponse(FeedRepository.kt:44)
    at okhttp3.internal.connection.RealCall$AsyncCall.run(RealCall.kt:519)

Line 88 is if (session != null) header.bind(session!!.displayName). session is var session: Session? = null on the presenter. The 8.4 diff added "logout on 401", which sets session = null from an auth callback. 70% of crashes come from users on flaky networks. The same release bumped OkHttp, and that is what the team is looking at.
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong, why did the compiler "allow" it, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "OkHttp upgrade broke something, roll it back," or "add ?. instead of !!." The first chases the red herring. The second hides the crash and shows a blank header without asking why two threads touch presenter state at all.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which threads call onFeedLoaded and the 401 handler? The stack shows OkHttp's dispatcher thread, not main. That matters.
    • Did 8.4 also change where the response callback runs? This rules OkHttp in or out.
    • Is the crash concentrated on sessions with a 401 just before it? Check breadcrumbs. This would confirm the logout race.
    • Any other !! on var properties added in this diff?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Kill switch the "logout on 401" flag, if it's behind one. Otherwise hotfix line 88 to snapshot into a local and return early. That stops the crash while I fix the threading.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Check-then-act race: line 88 reads session twice (check, then !!). The 401 handler on another thread nulls it in between. This matches the compiler's own smart-cast error, which someone silenced with !!.
    2. Callbacks running on the OkHttp thread and touching UI state. Even without the race, this is a threading bug that's waiting to happen.
    3. OkHttp upgrade changed callback ordering. It's unlikely to cause an NPE by itself and it's the red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics breadcrumbs and custom keys (log the 401 timestamp next to the crash). A unit test that runs onFeedLoaded and logout() concurrently in a loop with a CountDownLatch to force the interleaving. Check the decompiled bytecode of line 88: it shows two separate getSession()/field reads. Revert only the OkHttp bump in a test build to show the crash still reproduces.
  5. Root cause: session is a var property, so Kotlin refuses a smart cast, because another writer can change it. The developer added !!, which turns the compile-time guarantee into a runtime bet. The new logout path made the bet lose on slow networks, where a 401 and a feed response arrive close together on different threads.
  6. Fix: 
    // short-term
fun renderHeader() {
    val s = session ?: return       // single read, stable local
    header.bind(s.displayName)
}
    Long-term: give the presenter one thread. Move callbacks to main, or better, move this screen to a ViewModel exposing StateFlow<FeedUiState>, so the session is part of immutable state and is read once per render. The concurrency tools for this are in chunk C8.
  7. Prevention: A detekt rule or code-review checklist: no !! on a property read, especially after a null check (UnsafeCallOnNullableType in detekt flags !! usage). A Crashlytics alert on new NPE clusters. A test for the logout-during-load race.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I would not wrap everything in synchronized as a quick fix, because it hides the design problem and risks contention on main. I wouldn't blanket-replace !! with ?., because silent no-ops make UI bugs harder to see. And I wouldn't roll back OkHttp, since the evidence doesn't support it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if session were @Volatile?" → Visibility improves, but the race doesn't go away. It's still two reads. The local snapshot is what fixes it.
  • "Could K2 smart-cast this now?" → No. K2 never smart-casts var properties.
  • "What if render must show 'logged out' instead of returning?" → when (val s = session) { null -> showLoggedOut(); else -> bind(s) }. One read, both branches handled.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a past team, a pre-release grep for !! directly after != null checks on properties found 23 occurrences across the codebase. Three were already crashing at low rates nobody had prioritized.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames OkHttp, or suggests ?. without explaining the race.
  • Hire: Identifies the double read and the !! overriding the smart-cast refusal, and fixes with a local val.
  • Strong hire: Also spots the off-main callback threading, proposes single-threaded state, and adds a lint/test guardrail.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout screen (cart sizes 1 to 40 items). QA reports: "Total shows ₹49 for a ₹1,200 cart" and "audit log missing for guest users". The code:

data class Cart(val subtotal: Int?, val items: List<Item>)

fun total(cart: Cart?, shipping: Int): Int =
    cart?.subtotal ?: 0 + shipping

fun applyCoupon(order: Order?, code: String) {
    order?.coupon = couponService.redeem(code)   // redeem() also writes an audit record
}

fun isBigCart(cart: Cart?) = cart?.items?.size ?: 0 > 10

The ₹49 is the shipping fee. The team thinks the backend is sending a wrong subtotal.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and explain the exact evaluation rules behind each one.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Backend sends null subtotal sometimes." That's partly a red herring. The real problem is that the expression groups differently from what the author meant, and the person never looks at operator precedence or how the safe-call assignment evaluates.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When is subtotal null (loading state? guest?). Is order null for guests? Is redeem meant to run even for guests (does it consume the coupon server-side)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: This is not an incident yet. Block the release and add unit tests that pin down expected totals.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Precedence. Elvis binds more loosely than arithmetic. a ?: 0 + shipping parses as a ?: (0 + shipping). When subtotal is non-null, shipping is never added. When it's null, the total is only shipping. Both cases are wrong. ₹49 is the null case.
    2. Safe-call assignment. In order?.coupon = redeem(code), the right-hand side is evaluated only when order is non-null. That's documented Kotlin behavior. For guests (order == null), redeem and its audit write never run.
    3. cart?.items?.size ?: 0 > 10. Elvis binds tighter than comparison, so this is (size ?: 0) > 10, which is what the author meant. It's correct but unclear, so it's a red herring for a bug but worth parenthesizing.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write unit tests: total(Cart(1200, items), 49) should be 1249 and returns 1200. total(Cart(null, items), 49) returns 49. For the coupon, a fake couponService counts calls with order = null. In the IDE, "Add clarifying parentheses" (an intention action) shows how the parser grouped the expression.
  5. Root cause: Kotlin's precedence order is, from tighter to looser: multiplicative, additive, range, infix calls, elvis, in/is, comparison, equality, &&, ||. So ?: sits below + but above >. Separately, with a safe call on the left side of an assignment, the whole assignment, right side included, is skipped when the receiver is null.
  6. Fix: 
    fun total(cart: Cart?, shipping: Int): Int = (cart?.subtotal ?: 0) + shipping

fun applyCoupon(order: Order?, code: String) {
    val redeemed = couponService.redeem(code)   // runs regardless, if that's the requirement
    order?.coupon = redeemed
}

fun isBigCart(cart: Cart?) = (cart?.items?.size ?: 0) > 10
    Also question the model: why is subtotal nullable? A Cart in a loading state should be a different UI state, not a cart with a null subtotal.
  7. Prevention: A team style rule: always parenthesize elvis when it's mixed with other operators. Unit tests on money math with null and non-null inputs. Never hide side effects in the right-hand side of a safe-call assignment.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't "fix" it by changing the backend to never send null without also fixing the expression. The code is wrong either way. And I wouldn't turn every nullable into !! to "fail fast" on money paths. Model the states instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What about a ?: b ?: c + 1?" → It's a ?: (b ?: (c + 1)). Elvis is right-associative, and + binds tighter.
  • "Does a?.b += 1 evaluate anything when a is null?" → No. The compound assignment is skipped entirely.
  • "Does expensive() ?: fallback() call expensive() twice?" → No. The left side is evaluated once into a temporary, and fallback() runs only if that result is null.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite pattern from billing code: an elvis default sat inside a sum for months. It was only wrong on the "subtotal unavailable" path, so it slipped past happy-path tests until a promo increased the number of carts loaded from a stale cache.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doesn't find the precedence issue, or blames the backend.
  • Hire: Finds the precedence bug and the skipped right-hand side in the safe-call assignment.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the precedence order (elvis below additive, above comparison), questions the nullable subtotal model, and sets a parenthesizing rule plus tests.

questions.promptHtml: Where exactly do NPEs come from when Kotlin calls Java? Walk through the different failure points and how you'd design the boundary.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Q004 checks the definition. This one checks whether you can find the failing line from a stack trace and design an interop layer that keeps nulls out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "There are four ways it goes wrong. First, I dereference a platform value: a plain JVM NPE at that line. Second, I assign or pass a platform value into a declared non-null Kotlin type: a Kotlin-generated check throws 'X must not be null' at that line. Third, I override a Java method with non-null params and Java passes null: a checkNotNullParameter NPE at method entry. Fourth, a Java collection has null elements but I typed it List<String>: nothing checks, and it crashes wherever I use the element. My boundary rule: at every Java seam, declare explicit Kotlin types, nullable unless the Java side is annotated or documented non-null, and convert in one adapter layer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Java SDK  ──returns T!──▶  [ Kotlin adapter ]  ──T / T?──▶  domain / UI
                 ▲               │
                 │               ├─ explicit type: val x: String? = sdk.foo()
                 │               ├─ validate: x ?: return Result.failure(...)
Java callback ◀──┘               └─ overrides: param types follow the Java annotations
  • Failure 1, a dereference: sdk.getUser().name.length. The NPE stack trace points at Kotlin, but the bug is in the contract with Java.
  • Failure 2, assignment checks: they happen immediately, at the boundary. This is good, and it's why explicit types at seams help.
  • Failure 3, overrides: Android examples include onCreateView(inflater, container: ViewGroup?, ...). container really is nullable. When you override a Java interface or class, the IDE generates types from annotations. If the Java side is unannotated, you decide, so pick nullable unless you're certain.
  • Failure 4, generics and arrays: (Mutable)List<String!>!. Element nullability isn't checked. Java Map.get returns a platform V!, and getOrDefault behaves differently from Kotlin's getOrElse.
  • Static String! values flow through Kotlin vals and generic containers without anyone checking them. That's why the failure can be several frames away from the source.
  • Kotlin calling java.util.Optional: optional.orElse(null) gives T!. Declare it T?. Kotlin also has getOrNull() as an extension on Optional (kotlin.jvm.optionals, stdlib 1.8+).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Adapter around an unannotated Java SDK
class LocationGateway(private val sdk: LegacyGeoSdk) {
    fun lastFix(): Fix? {
        val raw: GeoFix? = sdk.getLastFix()          // explicit nullable: no platform type leaks out
        val provider: String? = raw?.getProvider()
        return raw?.let { Fix(it.getLat(), it.getLng(), provider ?: "unknown") }
    }
}

// Override of a Java listener: choose nullability deliberately
class Listener : LegacyGeoSdk.Callback {
    override fun onFix(fix: GeoFix?, error: String?) { /* handle both nulls */ }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Exposing platform types from your own public Kotlin API (fun token() = sdk.token). Callers inherit the uncertainty. detekt's HasPlatformType rule flags this.
  • Trusting Javadoc ("never returns null") over code across SDK upgrades.
  • Typing Java collections as non-null elements and then calling .sortedBy { it.name } on them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the stack trace often point deep inside Kotlin code? → Because the platform value spread through inference and was only dereferenced later.
  2. Does a null platform value always crash? → No. A string template "$x" or println(x) prints "null" without crashing, so a null can quietly reach a server payload or a UI label. That's often worse than a crash.
  3. How do you handle a Java method returning an array with possible null entries? → Array<out T?>. Declare it explicitly and filterNotNull() at the boundary.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "Java can return null, so use ?.." The senior lists the four failure modes, explains why the stack trace is misleading, and proposes an adapter layer with explicit types plus a lint guard on platform-type exposure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that wrap every Java SDK behind a small Kotlin gateway with explicit nullable types usually see far fewer interop NPEs than teams calling SDKs directly from ViewModels.

questions.promptHtml: Which nullability annotations does the Kotlin compiler understand, and how strictly does it enforce them? How do you control that?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Mixed Java/Kotlin codebases live or die by annotation strategy. Seniors are expected to know the flags and the JSpecify direction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Kotlin reads a fixed set of annotation families from Java and turns annotated types into real T or T? instead of platform types. The families are JetBrains (org.jetbrains.annotations), AndroidX and the old Android support annotations, JSR-305 (javax.annotation), FindBugs, Eclipse, Lombok @NonNull, RxJava 3, Vert.x, and JSpecify (org.jspecify.annotations). How hard a violation hits depends on the family. JSpecify mismatches are errors by default in current Kotlin. Most others can be set per package with -Xnullability-annotations=@pkg:ignore|warn|strict. JSR-305 has its own -Xjsr305 flag. For new Java code I'd use JSpecify with @NullMarked."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• How it's treated:
Family Default handling Control
JSpecify (@Nullable, @NonNull, @NullMarked, @NullUnmarked) strict (errors), per current kotlinlang.org docs `-Xjspecify-annotations=strict
JSR-305 (@Nonnull(when=...), @CheckForNull, @TypeQualifierDefault) warn (-Xjsr305=warn behavior) `-Xjsr305=strict
JetBrains / AndroidX / Android / Eclipse / FindBugs / Lombok / Rx3 / Vert.x recognized. Kotlin treats annotated types as nullable/non-null -Xnullability-annotations=@<package>:<level>
  • Version caveat: current kotlinlang.org docs list JSpecify as strict by default. Its enforcement was tightened during the Kotlin 2.x line, and earlier versions reported warnings. For the other families, the docs don't state every default level, so check against your compiler version before you depend on it.
  • @NullMarked (JSpecify) makes every unannotated type in a class or package non-null by default, so you annotate only the @Nullable exceptions. @NullUnmarked turns a scope back into platform types. This is far less noisy than annotating every parameter.
  • JSR-305 @Nonnull(when = When.MAYBE/NEVER) means nullable, and When.UNKNOWN means platform type. @TypeQualifierDefault lets you write package-level defaults.
  • Android SDK: android.jar stubs carry nullability annotations. Newly annotated APIs ship first as @RecentlyNullable/@RecentlyNonNull, which Kotlin reports as warnings, and are later promoted to errors. That's why an SDK bump (compileSdk) can turn warnings into compile errors.
  • Type-use annotations (on generics like List<@Nullable String>) need Java 8+ targets and type-use-capable annotation versions (JetBrains annotations 15+ for TYPE_USE).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Java, package-info.java
@NullMarked
package com.app.legacy.payments;
import org.jspecify.annotations.NullMarked;

// Java class in that package
public class Wallet {
    public String id() { ... }                      // non-null by default
    public @Nullable String nickname() { ... }      // explicitly nullable
}
wallet.id().length              // OK: String
wallet.nickname().length        // error (strict): only safe or !! calls allowed on String?

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding @NonNull without enforcement in Java. The annotation is a promise, and nobody checks the Java implementation keeps it. Pair it with a null checker on the Java side (NullAway or Error Prone) if the module is long-lived.
  • Mixing families in one module and being surprised that some report errors and some report warnings.
  • Flipping -Xjsr305=strict on a big codebase in one PR. That's hundreds of errors with no migration plan (see Q014).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Kotlin emit annotations for Java to consume? → Yes. It emits @NotNull/@Nullable (JetBrains) on public signatures, so Java IDEs and tools see the nullability.
  2. Why prefer JSpecify? → It's a cross-vendor standard with precise semantics (generics, defaults through @NullMarked), and Kotlin enforces it strictly.
  3. What happens if an annotation is a lie? → The annotated type is trusted, the compiler inserts no extra checks for Kotlin-side uses of a "non-null" Java return, and you get a plain NPE at the dereference.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "Use @Nullable/@NonNull from AndroidX." The senior knows the per-family strictness, the flags, @NullMarked defaults, the @RecentlyNullable SDK mechanism, and that annotations are trusted, not verified.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A compileSdk bump that promotes @RecentlyNonNull to non-null can break builds with override signature errors, for example a parameter that's now non-null. Plan SDK bumps with that in mind.

questions.subtopic: Platform types from a Java SDK
questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (2M DAU) bumped a Java-only payments SDK from 4.2 to 4.3 in release 11.0. 36 hours after a 20% rollout, the crash rate went from 0.15% to 1.2% of sessions on the checkout screen:

java.lang.NullPointerException: getSessionToken(...) must not be null
    at com.app.pay.PaymentRepository.startCheckout(PaymentRepository.kt:41)
    at com.app.pay.CheckoutViewModel$pay$1.invokeSuspend(CheckoutViewModel.kt:77)

Line 41 is val token: String = sdk.getSession().getSessionToken(). 62% of crashes are on Samsung Android 14 devices. The same release also changed R8 keep rules. The SDK changelog says: "Session initialization is now lazy and asynchronous."
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this and fix it, both now and structurally.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "R8 stripped something, add a keep rule," or "it's a Samsung bug." Neither explains the message. "must not be null" is a Kotlin-generated check on a platform-typed assignment, and the changelog explains why the token is null now.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the crash only on cold starts going straight to checkout? A lazy init race would show that.
    • Why is Samsung over-represented? It could be our user mix on those devices (the payment flow is popular on them) or faster cold-start paths.
    • Does the SDK expose an init callback or an isReady()?
    • Is the R8 change to SDK classes or unrelated? Check mapping.txt and the keep rules diff.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at 20%. If there's a remote config, route checkout to the old flow or show a "retry" state. I'd prioritize a hotfix that treats the token as nullable over pinning SDK 4.2, since 4.2 may hit end-of-life.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. SDK 4.3 returns null from getSessionToken() until async init completes. Our code assigns a platform type to a declared non-null String, so the inserted checkNotNullExpressionValue throws. The message format matches exactly.
    2. R8 obfuscation broke SDK reflection, which leaves the session uninitialized. Possible, but that usually shows up as ClassNotFound/NoSuchMethod, and the stack doesn't point at that.
    3. A Samsung-specific SDK behavior. This is more likely a correlation (device mix, faster startup) than the cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a debug build that cold-starts directly into the checkout deep link. Log sdk.isInitialized and the timestamp before line 41. Build a variant with the old R8 rules and the new SDK: if it still crashes, R8 is eliminated. Check Crashlytics custom keys for time-since-app-start at the crash, and expect most crashes under 2s.
  5. Root cause: getSessionToken() has no nullability annotation, so Kotlin sees String!. Declaring val token: String made the compiler insert a check that the old SDK never failed (it initialized synchronously). Once the SDK became asynchronous, a null shows up during the init window, and our boundary check fires. The check did its job and fired at the boundary. The bug is our assumption.
  6. Fix: 
    // short-term: treat as nullable, wait for readiness
suspend fun startCheckout(): CheckoutResult {
    val token: String = sdk.getSession().getSessionToken()
        ?: awaitSdkReady(timeoutMs = 3_000)
        ?: return CheckoutResult.SdkUnavailable
    return api.checkout(token)
}
    Here awaitSdkReady wraps the SDK's init callback (the callback interop pattern is in chunk C10). Long-term: a PaymentsGateway adapter that is the only class touching the SDK, with every return typed explicitly (String?) and mapped into a sealed result. Contract tests run against each SDK version before we bump.
  7. Prevention: detekt HasPlatformType on our public APIs. A rule that no SDK type escapes the gateway module. A pre-bump checklist: read the changelog for init/threading changes. Crash alerting per rollout percentage.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't add -Xno-call-assertions to "stop the crash". The NPE would move to a worse place, like inside the network call, or be silent with a null token sent to the server. I wouldn't runCatching the whole checkout either, since that swallows real failures and, in coroutine code, cancellation (chunk C5).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if we had written val token = ... with no type?" → It would be String!. It would pass into api.checkout(token), crash in Retrofit's serialization or send "null", and the stack trace would be further from the cause.
  • "SDK vendor says they'll annotate in 4.4. Does that help?" → Yes. With @Nullable, the compiler forces handling. Make sure the annotation family they choose is recognized (Q011).
  • "Why 1.2% and not 100%?" → Only cold starts that reach checkout inside the init window hit it. That's a timing race.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an SDK "made init async" in a minor version. Teams that had wrapped it behind a gateway changed one file. Teams calling it from 14 places shipped three hotfixes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doesn't recognize the Kotlin-generated message, or chases R8 or Samsung without evidence.
  • Hire: Explains the platform type plus the inserted check, ties it to the async init, and fixes with a nullable type and readiness handling.
  • Strong hire: Adds a gateway/adapter design, rollout discipline, and lint on platform types, and explains why disabling assertions would make things worse.

questions.promptHtml: Can a value declared as a non-null Kotlin type ever be null at runtime? List the ways, and say which ones the compiler-inserted checks catch.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers need an accurate model of where the guarantee ends. "Kotlin has no NPEs" is a red flag answer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Yes. Null safety is a compile-time guarantee about Kotlin code, plus runtime checks only at function entry and at platform-type assignments. Nulls get in through Java callers writing fields directly, Java subclasses overriding a Kotlin method and returning null, reflection-based deserializers that skip constructors, generic containers filled by Java, unchecked casts on erased generics, and reading a property before it's initialized during construction. The inserted checks catch Java calling non-private functions with null and platform values assigned to non-null types. They don't catch fields, reflection, generic contents, or override return values."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Entry path Example Caught by an inserted check?
Java calls a Kotlin function with null repo.save(null) from Java Yes, checkNotNullParameter at entry
Platform return stored as non-null val s: String = javaApi.get() Yes, checkNotNullExpressionValue
Java writes a public field @JvmField var name: String set to null from Java No
Java subclass overrides a Kotlin open fun name(): String and returns null Kotlin caller calls obj.name() No. The return type is Kotlin-declared, so no check at the call site
Reflection or Unsafe instantiation Gson creating objects without calling the constructor (details in chunk K1b) No
Generic contents from Java List<String> holding nulls No
Unchecked cast on erased types listOfAny as List<String> (warning) No. Fails later, at use
Initialization order an open member called from a superclass constructor reads a subclass property that isn't assigned yet (chunk K2b) No
Compiler flags -Xno-param-assertions, -Xno-call-assertions Checks removed
JNI / native code native code returns null into a non-null Kotlin declaration No
  • The design principle is that checks sit at "trust boundaries the compiler can see": function entries and expressions of platform type. Anything that bypasses a function call or a typed expression, such as fields, reflection and erased generics, bypasses the checks.
  • The result is that the NPE often shows up far from the cause, and that's the debugging challenge.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
open class Named { open fun name(): String = "kotlin" }
class JavaNamed extends Named {
    @Override public String name() { return null; }   // legal Java
}
fun greet(n: Named) = "Hi ${n.name().length}"   // NPE here; no Intrinsics check at the call site

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Arguing "it's declared String, so it can't be null" during a crash investigation.
  • Using @JvmField on public mutable properties in an API that Java consumes.
  • Calling as List<String> on decoded JSON maps and trusting the element types.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't Kotlin check return values of Kotlin-declared methods at call sites? → It would mean a check on every call, everywhere. The design trusts Kotlin-declared signatures and guards only the boundaries where the compiler knows Java is involved.
  2. How would you harden a library's public API for Java consumers? → Avoid public @JvmField on non-null references, make classes final where possible, validate in constructors, and emit @NotNull annotations (Kotlin does this automatically) so Java tools warn.
  3. Does K2 change any of this? → No. K2 changed smart casts and analysis, not the runtime-check model.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer mentions Java and !!. The senior gives the full table, explains why checks sit where they do, and uses it to triage a "null in a non-null type" crash quickly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "NPE on a non-null field" crash groups usually come down to reflection-based deserialization or Java subclasses in legacy modules, not Kotlin code.

questions.contextHtml: A ride-hailing app has a 180k-LOC Java module :legacy-core (pricing, trips, user). 70% of feature work is now Kotlin, calling into it. Over the last 90 days, 41% of all NPE crashes (about 0.09% of sessions out of 3M DAU) originate at Kotlin/Java seams in this module. A spike PR adding JSpecify @NullMarked to every package and building with default (strict) JSpecify handling produced 1,140 Kotlin compile errors across 9 feature modules. Releases go out weekly. The team can't freeze features.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration. How do you get the safety without a big-bang PR or breaking the weekly train?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add @Nullable/@NonNull everywhere and fix the errors." That's a 1,140-error PR that conflicts with every feature branch, and the annotations would be guesses. Wrong annotations are worse than none, because Kotlin trusts them.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which packages produce the most seam crashes? That gives a Pareto ordering.
    • Is there a Java-side null checker (NullAway or Error Prone) available in the build?
    • Are there Java consumers outside the app, such as an SDK, where annotation changes affect API?
    • What's the CI budget? A per-module compiler flag change should cost nothing.
  2. Immediate mitigation: This isn't an incident. Abandon the spike PR and keep its error list as a burn-down inventory.
  3. Hypotheses (plan options), ranked:
    1. Incremental @NullMarked, one package at a time, starting with the top crashers (pricing and trip, by Crashlytics). Verify each package on the Java side, then annotate.
    2. Temporarily lower JSpecify enforcement to warnings (-Xjspecify-annotations=warn) in consuming modules, so annotated packages land without breaking callers. Then ratchet back to strict module by module.
    3. Big-bang with strict mode. Rejected: merge conflicts and guessed annotations.
  4. How I'd verify each: Track the number of JSpecify warnings per module in CI, as a burn-down chart. Run NullAway on :legacy-core, so the Java implementation is checked against its own annotations. Watch Crashlytics NPE clusters by package before and after each wave. A release-over-release dashboard should show seam NPEs falling.
  5. Root cause (of the current crash load): Unannotated Java gives platform types. Kotlin callers guessed nullability, and the guesses were wrong in exactly the places where the crashes are.
  6. Fix:
    • Wave plan: about 6 packages per sprint, highest crash count first. For each package: add @NullMarked in package-info.java, mark real nullable returns and params as @Nullable (from code reading plus NullAway findings), and fix that package's Kotlin callers in the same PR. That's roughly 50 to 150 errors per PR instead of 1,140.
    • Build config while migrating:
    // feature module build.gradle.kts, temporary
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.add("-Xjspecify-annotations=warn")
    }
}
    Remove the flag module by module once its warning count is 0, and fail CI if it comes back.
    • Packages not yet migrated stay unmarked, so they stay platform types and behave exactly as today. @NullUnmarked is an escape hatch for a class we can't verify yet.
  7. Prevention: Make NullAway in :legacy-core mandatory for marked packages. Add a CI check that new Java files in the module are @NullMarked. Use detekt HasPlatformType on Kotlin public API. Track seam NPEs per release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't annotate from Javadoc alone. A wrong @NonNull removes the Kotlin developer's prompt to handle null, and Kotlin won't insert a check for it.
    • I wouldn't use -Xjsr305=strict with JSR-305 as the main path. JSpecify is the maintained standard with clearer generics semantics.
    • Running in warn mode for weeks is a risk if people ignore warnings. The ratchet in CI is what makes it work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not convert :legacy-core to Kotlin instead?" → Long-term, maybe. But conversion under live traffic risks behavior changes. Annotation is cheap, reversible, and makes the eventual conversion mechanical.
  • "A Java method returns null only in an error path. Is it @Nullable?" → Yes. If it can ever return null, it's nullable. Otherwise, change it to throw and document it.
  • "What happens to Kotlin code calling a now-@NullMarked method with ?.?" → It gets a warning for an unnecessary safe call. That's harmless and cleans up over time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team that annotated its top five crash packages first removed most seam NPEs within two releases. The remaining packages took a year and mattered much less.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang annotation, or "just convert to Kotlin".
  • Hire: Incremental by package, prioritized by crash data, uses a warn mode and fixes callers per PR.
  • Strong hire: Adds Java-side verification (NullAway), explains why a wrong annotation is dangerous, sets a CI ratchet, and measures the result per release.

questions.contextHtml:
You're leading the post-incident review. A food-delivery app (800k DAU) had a 3-hour window where crash-free sessions dropped from 99.7% to 98.9%. Timeline: the backend shipped a new order status "REASSIGNED" at 18:05. The app crashed when opening order tracking:

kotlin.NotImplementedError: An operation is not implemented: map REASSIGNED later
    at com.app.orders.StatusMapper.map(StatusMapper.kt:23)
    at com.app.orders.OrderRepository.track(OrderRepository.kt:58)

The code:

fun map(raw: String): OrderStatus = when (raw) {
    "PLACED" -> OrderStatus.Placed
    "PICKED" -> OrderStatus.Picked
    "DELIVERED" -> OrderStatus.Delivered
    else -> TODO("map $raw later")
}

// OrderRepository.track
try { emitStatus(mapper.map(dto.status)) } catch (e: Exception) { emitStatus(OrderStatus.Unknown) }

Someone says, "But we have a try/catch, so this can't crash." The backend team is being blamed for the deploy.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review. What's the real root cause, and what changes do you drive?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Backend shouldn't ship new values without telling us," and "replace TODO with a default." That's half right. It misses why the try/catch didn't help and why a type-system feature turned a planned placeholder into a crash.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Was the API contract documented as an open set? Most status enums are, so the app has to tolerate unknown values.
    • How did TODO() pass review? Was there any lint?
    • Why 3 hours? Did the backend roll back, or did someone ship a hotfix? What was our time to detect?
    • Do other mappers have the same pattern?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what happened or should have): Backend rolls back or hides REASSIGNED from older app versions using a version header. The app ships a hotfix that maps unknown values to Unknown.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. TODO() returns Nothing and throws NotImplementedError, which extends Error, not Exception. So catch (e: Exception) doesn't catch it.
    2. The client assumed a closed set of values from an open server contract.
    3. Backend deploy process. It's a contributing factor, not the root cause. The client has to be robust to new values anyway.
  4. How I'd verify each: The stack trace shows NotImplementedError. The stdlib source shows class NotImplementedError : Error. A unit test calling map("NEW") inside catch (e: Exception) still fails. Grep and detekt across the repo for TODO( in non-test sources.
  5. Root cause: TODO() type-checks anywhere because its return type is Nothing, so the compiler accepted it as a valid OrderStatus branch. That's exactly what makes it convenient as a placeholder and dangerous in shipping code. At runtime it throws an Error, which skips Exception handlers by design, because Error signals "should not happen". Combined with an else branch that treated unknown input as "not implemented" rather than as data, the first new server value crashed every tracking screen.
  6. Fix: 
    fun map(raw: String): OrderStatus = when (raw) {
    "PLACED" -> OrderStatus.Placed
    "PICKED" -> OrderStatus.Picked
    "DELIVERED" -> OrderStatus.Delivered
    else -> OrderStatus.Unknown(raw).also { logger.warn("unknown status $raw") } // data, not a bug
}
    Long-term: unknown values are a modeled state in every server enum mapping, with UI fallback copy. Non-fatal logging tells us when the server adds values.
  7. Prevention:
    • detekt NotImplementedDeclaration set to fail CI on TODO() in main source sets.
    • A review checklist item: "every server-enum mapping has an unknown branch".
    • Contract tests using a fixture with an unrecognized value.
    • An agreed API rule: new enum values ship behind a minimum-app-version gate.
    • Alerting: a crash-free drop of more than 0.2% inside 15 minutes pages on-call. That would have cut the 3 hours.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't change the catch to catch (t: Throwable). Catching Error hides OutOfMemoryError and similar, and a broad catch can swallow coroutine cancellation (chunk C5).
    • I wouldn't make the review about blaming backend. The fix that keeps us safe has to be on the client.
    • I'd keep error("...") (an IllegalStateException) for truly impossible internal states, not for external input.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "What if the mapper returned OrderStatus? with else -> null?" → It works, but then null means "unknown" implicitly, and callers end up inventing their own defaults. An explicit Unknown(raw) state is clearer.
  • "Would a sealed class or enum on the client have caught this at compile time?" → No. Exhaustiveness covers client-side types, not server strings. The boundary mapping is where unknowns have to be handled.
  • "Would runCatching have caught it?" → Yes. runCatching catches Throwable, Errors included. That's exactly why it's a dangerous default (it also catches CancellationException).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a TODO() placeholder sat behind a feature flag for months. Flipping the flag server-side in one region took down a screen for every user there within minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames backend, doesn't know NotImplementedError is an Error.
  • Hire: Explains Nothing/TODO typing, Error vs Exception, and adds an unknown branch.
  • Strong hire: Drives systemic fixes (lint gate, contract tests, version-gated enum rollout, alert thresholds) and explains why catching Throwable is the wrong fix.

questions.subtopic: Smart casts across modules & custom getters
questions.contextHtml:
A team is splitting a monolith app into 48 Gradle modules. After moving Config, UserSession and the model classes into :core:model, the feature modules show 640 errors like:

Smart cast to 'String' is impossible, because 'config.cdnHost' is a public API property declared in different module.

A senior dev proposes a codemod that adds !! at all 640 sites "since the code worked before". Another proposes making the models internal with @PublishedApi tricks. Meanwhile, Config.cdnHost is declared as val cdnHost: String? get() = remoteConfig.getString("cdn").takeIf { it.isNotBlank() }. Remote config refreshes in the background every 12 hours.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend and why? Explain what the compiler is protecting against.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run the !! codemod, it's equivalent to the old behavior." It isn't. Some of those properties have custom getters, so the old code already read them twice. And the codemod hides future breakage when the property's implementation changes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • How many of the 640 sites read properties with custom getters or open properties? Those were already unsound before the split.
    • Are the model classes plain data (data class with constructor vals) or behavior-heavy?
    • Is the module split final, or are we iterating?
    • Are there current crashes in the custom-getter properties?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the split branch unmerged until the fix approach is chosen. There's no production impact yet.
  3. Hypotheses (options), ranked:
    1. Snapshot into locals at the use site (val host = config.cdnHost ?: return). It's mechanical, correct, and IntelliJ can do it per site.
    2. Move behavior to where the data lives. If 30 call sites do if (session.user != null) session.user.name, add val displayName: String or fun displayNameOrNull() on the model, so callers stop doing null-and-use pairs.
    3. Rethink the nullability. Some properties are nullable only because of how they're initialized. Making them non-null (constructor-required) removes the check entirely.
    4. !! codemod: rejected. 4b, internal visibility tricks: rejected. Models have to be public across modules, and fighting visibility is a design smell.
  4. How I'd verify each: Script the 640 errors by property and by whether the property has a custom getter or is open (a quick PSI or grep pass). Pick 3 high-count properties for option 2 and measure the error reduction. For cdnHost, write a test where remote config changes between two reads and show the two-read code observing different values.
  5. Root cause: Smart casts need a stable value. A public val from another module isn't stable to the compiler. That module could change it to a custom getter later, and dependent modules aren't necessarily recompiled with it (binary compatibility). Within the monolith, the compiler could see the final backing field and allowed it. cdnHost shows the compiler is right: it has a getter that re-reads remote config. Even in the monolith, the smart cast wasn't allowed for it, so those sites already had a !! or ?.let, and any !! there can race with the 12-hour refresh.
  6. Fix: 
    // use site
fun imageUrl(path: String): String? {
    val host = config.cdnHost ?: return null          // one read, stable
    return "https://$host/$path"
}

// model side: make the computation explicit and cheap to reason about
class Config(private val rc: RemoteConfig) {
    fun cdnHostOrNull(): String? = rc.getString("cdn").takeIf { it.isNotBlank() } // a function signals "computed"
}
    I'd also prefer fun over a custom-getter val for anything that does I/O or can change between reads. A property suggests a cheap, stable read.
  7. Prevention: A team guideline: custom getters only for cheap derivations from immutable state. Ban !! codemods (detekt UnsafeCallOnNullableType with a baseline). Modularization playbook: before moving models, audit nullable public properties.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • The local-val approach adds some lines at 640 sites, but it's correct, and IDE quick-fixes make it cheap.
    • Turning on a compiler option to "allow" these smart casts isn't possible. No such flag exists, and you'd be asking for unsound behavior.
    • I wouldn't merge the modules back just to recover smart casts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Would data class constructor vals be smart-castable cross-module?" → No. The rule is about module boundaries, not how the property is declared. Kotlin still refuses, because the declaring module could change it.
  • "Does K2 make this go away?" → No. K2 improved smart casts within a function's flow, but kept the cross-module stability rule.
  • "Is ?.let {} better than a local val here?" → Same correctness. Pick by readability. Deep let nesting is worse (chunk K4).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after a modularization, a team that refactored repeated null-and-use pairs into model methods cut the error count by more than half before any manual edits, and the code read better afterward.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Accepts the !! codemod.
  • Hire: Explains the cross-module stability rule and uses local snapshots.
  • Strong hire: Identifies the custom-getter race, pushes behavior onto models, distinguishes fun vs val semantics, and sets guidelines for the rest of the modularization.

questions.promptHtml: When you design a Kotlin API, how do you decide between returning T?, throwing (a Nothing-typed path), or returning a richer result type? What conventions does the stdlib follow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors design APIs that others call thousands of times. This shows judgment, not just syntax knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I return T? when absence is a normal, single-meaning outcome. A lookup miss is the classic case, and the caller can handle it in one ?:. I throw when the caller broke a precondition or the state is impossible, using require, check or error, whose Nothing paths smart-cast cleanly. When there's more than one way to fail, or the caller needs the reason, I return a sealed result instead of null. The stdlib convention is pairs: first() throws and firstOrNull() returns null. getOrNull, getOrElse and getOrThrow work the same way. Name the nullable variant with OrNull, so the call site says what happens."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Situation Return Why
Lookup that may legitimately miss T? (findUser(id): User?) one meaning for null, cheap, and composes with ?:
Caller passed an invalid argument throw via require(...) → IllegalArgumentException a programmer error, so fail fast
Object in an illegal state check(...) / checkNotNull → IllegalStateException; error() an invariant broke
Multiple failure reasons (network, auth, parse) sealed result / Result<T> null can't carry the reason; see the error-handling chunks
Both styles needed pair: parse() throws, parseOrNull() returns null the caller picks; stdlib precedent (toInt/toIntOrNull)
  • Avoid Boolean? and "null means two things" APIs. If null can mean "not loaded" or "not found", model a sealed state instead.
  • Nullable collections: return an empty list rather than List<T>?, unless "unknown" is genuinely different from "empty".
  • Parameters: make them non-null by default. A nullable parameter with a default of null often hides two functions in one.
  • Guard helpers: require/check use contracts so the compiler smart-casts after them (require(x != null) makes x non-null). Contracts are covered in chunk K9.
  • Interop: Kotlin emits nullability annotations on public signatures, so Java callers see @Nullable returns. That's another reason to keep public types precise.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface UserStore {
    fun find(id: UserId): User?                    // miss is normal
    fun get(id: UserId): User =                     // caller asserts presence
        find(id) ?: throw NoSuchElementException("user $id not found")
}

fun transfer(amountPaise: Long, to: AccountId?) {
    require(amountPaise > 0) { "amount must be positive: $amountPaise" }
    requireNotNull(to) { "destination missing" }    // to: AccountId from here
    // ...
}

sealed interface LoadResult<out T> {
    data class Ok<T>(val value: T) : LoadResult<T>
    data object NotFound : LoadResult<Nothing>
    data class Failed(val cause: Throwable) : LoadResult<Nothing>
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Returning null for network errors. The caller can't tell "no data" from "offline", and the UI shows an empty state instead of an error.
  • Throwing from a lookup that commonly misses. That forces try/catch at every call site.
  • Nullable parameters and nullable returns everywhere "to be safe". That spreads uncertainty through the codebase.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. require vs check? → require is for arguments (IllegalArgumentException), check is for the object's or system's own state (IllegalStateException).
  2. Is kotlin.Result OK as a public return type? → It has been allowed as a return type since Kotlin 1.5. Note that runCatching catches cancellation, which is covered in the coroutine exception chunk.
  3. How do you evolve a nullable return into a richer result without breaking callers? → Add a new function (loadResult()), deprecate the old one with ReplaceWith, and migrate callers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer: "Return null if not found." The senior has a decision table, follows stdlib naming pairs, refuses null for multi-cause failures, and considers how Java callers and future API changes are affected.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Empty screen instead of error screen" bugs almost always come from a repository that returns null or emptyList() on network failure.

questions.contextHtml:
A performance squad on a large super-app (140 modules, ~95k Kotlin methods in release dex, cold start p50 1.9s on a Snapdragon 6-series reference device) proposes for release builds:

kotlin { compilerOptions { freeCompilerArgs.addAll("-Xno-param-assertions", "-Xno-call-assertions") } }

plus an R8 rule:

-assumenosideeffects class kotlin.jvm.internal.Intrinsics {
    public static void checkNotNullParameter(java.lang.Object, java.lang.String);
    public static void checkNotNullExpressionValue(java.lang.Object, java.lang.String);
}
